title: Ceres et Proserpina
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: This is the second half of Ovid's telling of Ceres and Proserpina, and it opens with the girl already gone. Ceres, still searching, comes back to Sicily and finds her daughter's sash floating in a pool; she takes her grief out on the island, breaking the ploughs and blighting the seed, until the spring-nymph Arethusa surfaces to tell her that she has seen Proserpina below — sorrowful, but a queen. Ceres goes up to Jupiter, and what follows is an argument between two parents over a daughter neither of them consults: the mother calls the man who took her a bandit, the father answers that, rightly named, it was not an outrage but love. The case is settled by a clause in the compact of the Fates and by seven pomegranate seeds the girl had already eaten. Around that turn the passage sets two transformations — the informer Ascalaphus into a screech-owl, and Proserpina's companions the Sirens into birds with girls' faces — and it closes by cutting the year in half, which is the Roman account of why the earth goes bare and comes back. The Latin is dactylic hexameter, and the sentences run freely across the verse lines, so the unit you tap usually spans two or three lines and often begins in the middle of one; the line numbers are the standard way to cite the poem. There is no text-to-speech for Latin here — reading is by eye.

advisory.lede: These lines are the aftermath of the rape of Proserpina: a girl seized and made the wife of the ruler of the dead, whose father then defends the seizure as love rather than injury.
advisory.more: The seizure itself is not re-enacted here, but it is what the whole part is about. Ceres calls the man who took her daughter a bandit and the act a robbery; Jupiter replies that if things are given their true names it was not an outrage but love, and that his brother is no disgrace as a son-in-law. Proserpina is never asked what she wants, and the settlement that closes the part splits her year between the two houses without her. The text is presented unaltered, and the translations keep Ceres' contempt and Jupiter's evasion at the strength the Latin gives them.

sentences.t:
Quas dea per terras et quas erraverit undas,
dicere longa mora est:
sentences.l:
Through what lands the goddess wandered and through what waters,
to tell is a long delay:
sentences.i: It would take too long to tell what lands and what seas the goddess wandered over.
sentences.n: Two indirect questions held out in front of their verb: 'quas per terras... et quas... undas erraverit' — 'through what lands and through what waves she wandered', with the perfect subjunctive 'erraverit' because the question is reported rather than asked. 'per' governs both accusatives. 'longa mora est' is an idiom — 'it is a long delay' = 'it would take too long' — and the infinitive 'dicere' is its subject.

sentences.t: quaerenti defuit orbis.
sentences.l: to her, seeking, the world ran short.
sentences.i: she ran out of world to search in.
sentences.n: 'desum' takes a dative of the person who goes without: 'orbis defuit quaerenti', 'the world was lacking to her as she searched'. 'quaerenti' is a present participle standing alone as a noun, 'to [the woman] searching'. 'orbis' is the circle of the earth, the whole world. Three words that turn a search into a boundary: not that she failed to find her, but that the world gave out first.

sentences.t:
Sicaniam repetit; dumque omnia lustrat eundo,
venit et ad Cyanen.
sentences.l:
She makes for Sicania again; and while she goes over everything as she goes,
she comes also to Cyane.
sentences.i: She heads back to Sicily; and as she ranges over every part of it, she comes to Cyane as well.
sentences.n: 'Sicania' is a poetic name for Sicily, after the Sicani who were said to have held it. 'repetit' is a present tense inside a past narrative — the historic present, which Ovid slips in and out of to quicken the telling. 'lustrat' means to traverse and survey at once, the verb used of an army reviewed or a district gone over. 'eundo' is the ablative gerund of 'eo', literally 'by going', where English says 'as she went'. Cyane is a Sicilian spring, and the name belongs both to the nymph and to the pool; what has become of her comes in the next lines.

sentences.t:
Ea ni mutata fuisset,
omnia narrasset: sed et os et lingua volenti
dicere non aderant, nec quo loqueretur habebat.
sentences.l:
Had she not been changed,
she would have told everything; but both mouth and tongue, for her wanting
to speak, were not there, nor did she have [anything] with which she might speak.
sentences.i: Had she not been transformed she would have told the whole story; but she wanted to speak and there was no mouth, no tongue — nothing left her to speak with.
sentences.n: A past contrary-to-fact condition: 'ni mutata fuisset... narrasset', 'if she had not been changed... she would have told', both verbs pluperfect subjunctive ('narrasset' is the shortened form of 'narravisset'). 'volenti dicere' is a dative participle, 'for her, wishing to speak'. 'nec quo loqueretur habebat' — 'nor did she have [that] with which she might speak': 'quo' is an ablative of means, and the subjunctive marks a clause of characteristic, describing the kind of thing she lacks. 'et... et' is 'both... and'.

sentences.t:
Signa tamen manifesta dedit notamque parenti,
illo forte loco delapsam in gurgite sacro,
Persephones zonam summis ostendit in undis.
sentences.l:
Clear signs, nonetheless, she gave, and — known to the mother,
by chance slipped down in that place into the sacred pool —
Persephone's sash she showed on the top of the water.
sentences.i: Still, she gave clear signs: she showed on the surface of the water Persephone's sash, which her mother knew, and which had happened to slip off there into the sacred pool.
sentences.n: Everything in the sentence hangs on one word that arrives only in the last line: 'zonam', the sash. 'notam' ('known') and 'delapsam' ('having slipped down') are both accusative feminine agreeing with it. 'delabor' is deponent — passive in form, active in sense — so 'delapsam' means 'having fallen', not 'having been dropped'. 'Persephones' is a Greek genitive singular kept in its Greek shape. 'summis in undis': 'summus' means the top of whatever it agrees with, so 'at the surface of the water'. The zona is the girdle a Roman bride wore to be untied.

sentences.t:
Quam simul agnovit, tamquam tunc denique raptam
scisset, inornatos laniavit diva capillos
et repetita suis percussit pectora palmis.
sentences.l:
And as soon as she recognized it — as though only then at last
she had learned her snatched away — the goddess tore her unbound hair
and struck her breast, struck again, with her own palms.
sentences.i: The moment she knew it — as though only then, at last, she had learned the girl was stolen — the goddess tore at her loose hair and beat her breast again and again with her palms.
sentences.n: 'Quam' opens the sentence as a connecting relative: not 'which' but 'and it', reaching back to the sash. This is one of the commonest ways a Latin sentence starts, and you should read such a 'quam' or 'quae' as 'and her', 'and it'. 'tamquam... scisset' is an imagined comparison with the pluperfect subjunctive, 'as though she had learned'; inside it 'raptam' is an accusative with 'esse' left out, '[that her daughter had been] carried off'. 'repetita... pectora' is an economy English cannot copy: the participle 'repeated' is fastened to the breast rather than to the blows. 'inornatos' is hair left undressed — the hair of mourning already.

sentences.t:
Nescit adhuc, ubi sit: terras tamen increpat omnes
ingratasque vocat nec frugum munere dignas,
Trinacriam ante alias, in qua vestigia damni
repperit.
sentences.l:
She does not yet know where [the girl] is; yet she rails at all lands
and calls them ungrateful and unworthy of the gift of grain,
Trinacria before the others, in which she found the traces
of her loss.
sentences.i: She still does not know where the girl is; but she rails at every land on earth, calling them ungrateful and unfit for the gift of grain — Sicily before all the rest, since it was there she found the traces of what she had lost.
sentences.n: 'ubi sit' is an indirect question and so takes the subjunctive, 'where she is'. 'dignas' governs the ablative 'munere', 'worthy of the gift'. 'Trinacria' is Sicily under another poetic name, 'the three-cornered', from its three headlands — and it is the most fertile island in the goddess of grain's world, which is what makes the next lines what they are. 'damnum' is loss in the hard sense, the word a Roman would use of property gone. Watch the tenses: the presents 'nescit... increpat... vocat' put you beside her, and then the perfect 'repperit' drops back to the moment before.

sentences.t:
Ergo illic saeva vertentia glaebas
fregit aratra manu, parilique irata colonos
ruricolasque boves leto dedit arvaque iussit
fallere depositum vitiataque semina fecit.
sentences.l:
So there with savage hand she broke the ploughs that turn the clods,
and in her anger with a like hand gave the farmers
and the field-working oxen to death, and ordered the fields
to cheat their deposit, and made the seed spoiled.
sentences.i: So there she broke, with a savage hand, the ploughs that turn the soil; in her rage that same hand dealt death to the farmers and to the oxen that work the land; she ordered the fields to default on what had been entrusted to them, and she spoiled the seed.
sentences.n: 'saeva... manu' (savage hand) is split wide apart with 'vertentia glaebas... aratra' (the clod-turning ploughs) folded inside it — the ordinary shape of a verse line, adjective and noun at opposite ends. 'parili' is 'with a like [hand]', picking up 'manu' from the clause before. 'leto dedit', 'gave to death', is a fixed phrase for killing. The last two clauses turn farming into banking: a 'depositum' is money or goods lodged with someone for safekeeping, and to 'fallere' it is to default; the sown seed is a deposit the earth is ordered not to return. 'vitiata... fecit' is an object with a participle predicated of it, 'made the seed spoiled'.

sentences.t:
Fertilitas terrae latum vulgata per orbem
falsa iacet:
sentences.l:
The land's fertility, spread abroad through the wide world,
lies proved false:
sentences.i: That land's fertility, a byword the whole world over, is exposed as a lie:
sentences.n: 'vulgata' is from 'vulgus', the crowd — to make a thing common talk. 'iacet' is the verb for lying flat, of something brought down, and with 'falsa' ('false, shown up as false') it says both that the reputation is on the ground and that it was a lie all along. 'latum... per orbem' wraps itself round the participle it belongs with.

sentences.t:
primis segetes moriuntur in herbis,
et modo sol nimius, nimius modo corripit imber
sideraque ventique nocent, avidaeque volucres
semina iacta legunt;
sentences.l:
the crops die in the first blade,
and now too much sun, now too much rain seizes them,
and stars and winds do harm, and greedy birds
pick up the scattered seed;
sentences.i: the crops die while still in the blade; now it is too much sun, now too much rain that ruins them; stars and winds do their damage, and greedy birds gather up the sown seed;
sentences.n: 'primis in herbis' is 'in their first blades', while still seedlings. 'modo... modo' is 'now... now', and Ovid crosses the halves over the middle of the line — 'sol nimius, nimius... imber', sun too much, too much rain — so that the two disasters mirror each other. 'corripit' is singular though sun and rain are two: Latin lets a verb agree with the nearer subject, or take each in turn. The 'sidera' are blamed because the constellations set the farming calendar, so bad stars mean bad weather. 'noceo' usually takes a dative of what is harmed; here it stands bare, 'do harm'.

sentences.t:
lolium tribulique fatigant
triticeas messes et inexpugnabile gramen.
sentences.l:
darnel and caltrops wear down
the wheat harvests, and [so does] grass that cannot be stormed.
sentences.i: darnel and star-thistle wear the wheat crop down, and so does the grass that nothing can dislodge.
sentences.n: 'gramen' is a third subject arriving after the object, tacked on at the end as the worst of them — hence the '[so does]' supplied in the literal. 'lolium' is darnel, the weed that grows among grain and poisons the flour; 'tribulus' is the caltrop or star-thistle, whose three-spiked seed gave its name to the spiked iron dropped on the ground to lame cavalry. 'inexpugnabile' is a siege word, used of a town that cannot be taken by assault, put here on plain grass: the weeds are an army the field cannot throw off.

sentences.t:
Tum caput Eleis Alpheias extulit undis
rorantesque comas a fronte removit ad aures
atque ait:
sentences.l:
Then the Alphean woman lifted her head from the Elean waters
and moved her dripping hair back from her brow to her ears
and said:
sentences.i: Then the nymph of the Alpheus raised her head out of the waters of Elis, pushed her dripping hair back from her forehead behind her ears, and said:
sentences.n: 'Alpheias' is a Greek formation, 'the woman of the Alpheus' — the river of Elis in the Peloponnese. The ending names the river she is bound to, not a father; this part never gives her one. She gives her own name, Arethusa, only at 496. 'Eleis... undis' is an ablative of separation with 'extulit', 'carried out of', and that is the point of the two names: a spring in Sicily surfaces speaking out of Greek water. 'rorantes' is from 'ros', dew — hair that drips. 'a fronte... ad aures' traces the movement of the hand.

sentences.t:
“O toto quaesitae virginis orbe
et frugum genetrix, inmensos siste labores
neve tibi fidae violenta irascere terrae.
sentences.l:
“O mother of the maiden sought through the whole world
and of the crops, halt your measureless labours,
and do not, in your violence, be angry at a land faithful to you.
sentences.i: “Mother of the girl you have hunted for through the whole world, and mother of the crops — put an end to these endless labours, and do not turn your violence on a land that has kept faith with you.
sentences.n: 'genetrix' governs two genitives pulled far apart — 'virginis' at the end of one line, 'frugum' at the head of the next: mother of the daughter and mother of the grain, the two things Ceres is. 'toto... orbe' is an ablative of place wrapped round 'quaesitae virginis'. 'siste' is the imperative of 'sisto', to bring to a stand. 'neve... irascere' is a prohibition, 'irascere' being the present imperative of the deponent 'irascor', which takes a dative — 'terrae', itself described by a second dative, 'tibi fidae', 'faithful to you'. 'violenta' is a nominative adjective describing Ceres where English wants an adverb. Magnus spells 'inmensos' with n, not the later 'immensos'.

sentences.t: Terra nihil meruit patuitque invita rapinae.
sentences.l: The land earned nothing, and unwilling it lay open to the robbery.
sentences.i: The land did nothing to deserve this; it lay open to the theft against its will.
sentences.n: 'nihil meruit' is 'has deserved nothing' — has done nothing to earn what is being done to it. 'pateo' takes a dative of what is let in: 'patuit rapinae', 'lay open to the seizure'. 'invita' is once more a nominative adjective doing adverbial work, 'unwilling'. 'rapina' is the plain word for robbery, and it belongs to the same root as 'raptam' at 471 and 'rapta' at 520: on the nymph's lips the carrying-off of the daughter is named as a theft.

sentences.t:
Nec sum pro patria supplex: huc hospita veni;
Pisa mihi patria est et ab Elide ducimus ortus;
sentences.l:
Nor am I a suppliant on behalf of my own country: I came here a stranger;
Pisa is my country, and from Elis we draw our origin;
sentences.i: And I am not pleading for a country of my own: I came here as an incomer. Pisa is my homeland; it is from Elis that I trace my descent.
sentences.n: 'supplex' is noun and adjective at once — one who kneels — and 'pro patria' says on whose behalf. 'hospita' is the feminine of 'hospes', a word that covers guest, host and stranger alike; here 'as a foreigner'. Pisa is the town in Elis beside the Alpheus, not the Italian city. 'ducimus ortus' is 'we draw our beginnings': the plural is the poetic 'we' for 'I', which Latin verse uses freely, and 'ortus' is the accusative plural of a fourth-declension noun meaning risings, origins.

sentences.t:
Sicaniam peregrina colo, sed gratior omni
haec mihi terra solo est: hos nunc Arethusa penates,
hanc habeo sedem: quam tu, mitissima, serva.
sentences.l:
As a foreigner I dwell in Sicania, but this land is dearer to me
than any soil: these household gods now I, Arethusa,
this home I have — and it, most gentle one, do you keep safe.
sentences.i: I live in Sicily as an incomer, and yet this land is dearer to me than any ground on earth. These are the hearth-gods I have now, this is my home — keep it safe, you who are gentlest of all.
sentences.n: 'gratior... omni... solo' is a comparative with the ablative of comparison, 'dearer than every soil'. The 'penates' are the gods of the store-cupboard and so of the household: to name your Penates is to name where you belong. She gives her name in the middle of the sentence, in apposition to the 'I' inside the verb. 'quam' is another connecting relative, 'and it', reaching back to 'sedem', and 'serva' is the imperative of 'servo', keep, preserve. The superlative 'mitissima', 'gentlest', is addressed to a goddess who is at this moment killing farmers, and is meant to be heard.

sentences.t:
Mota loco cur sim tantique per aequoris undas
advehar Ortygiam, veniet narratibus hora
tempestiva meis, cum tu curaque levata
et vultus melioris eris.
sentences.l:
Why I was moved from my place, and through the waves of so great a sea
am carried to Ortygia — a fitting hour will come
for my tellings, when you are both lightened of care
and of a better face.
sentences.i: Why I was moved from where I belonged, and why I am carried over so wide a sea to Ortygia — there will be a right hour for that story of mine, when your care has been lifted and your face is brighter.
sentences.n: Two indirect questions, 'cur mota sim' and '[cur] advehar', both subjunctive, stand in front of the main clause, and English has to mark the suspension with a dash. 'narratibus... meis' is a dative, 'for my tellings'. 'curaque levata... eris' is 'you will be lightened of care', with the ablative of the thing taken away. 'vultus melioris' is a genitive of description, 'of a better expression', which Latin can hang on a person as a quality. Ortygia is the island of Syracuse, where the spring Arethusa rises. She offers the story and withholds it — within this part she never tells it.

sentences.t:
Mihi pervia tellus
praebet iter, subterque imas ablata cavernas
hic caput attollo desuetaque sidera cerno.
sentences.l:
For me the earth, having a way through,
provides a road, and, carried off beneath the lowest caverns,
here I lift my head and look on stars grown unfamiliar.
sentences.i: The earth is passable for me and gives me a road; swept along under the deepest caves, I come up here, lift my head, and see stars I have grown unused to.
sentences.n: 'pervia' is 'per' plus 'via', having a way through — the earth is a thing that can be gone through. 'ablata' is the perfect participle of 'aufero', carried away, describing her borne along by the water. 'desueta... sidera' is literally 'stars gone out of use': the unfamiliarity is really hers, not theirs, and Latin fastens the adjective to the stars. The literal leaves it where Latin puts it; the idiomatic moves it back onto her, 'stars I have grown unused to'.

sentences.t:
Ergo dum Stygio sub terris gurgite labor,
visa tua est oculis illic Proserpina nostris:
sentences.l:
So then, while I glide beneath the earth in the Stygian flood,
your Proserpina was seen there by our eyes:
sentences.i: And so, as I glide beneath the earth in the water of the Styx, I saw your Proserpina down there with my own eyes:
sentences.n: 'labor' here is a verb, first person singular of the deponent 'labi', to glide or slip along — spelled exactly like the noun 'labor', toil, which stood in the plural at 490. Only the context tells them apart. 'dum' keeps its present tense even inside a past narrative. 'visa est' is the perfect passive of 'video': Latin prefers 'she was seen by our eyes' where English prefers 'I saw her', and 'nostris' is the poetic plural for 'my' again. 'tua... Proserpina' and 'oculis... nostris' are interlocked across the line — 'visa tua est oculis illic Proserpina nostris' — so that the daughter stands inside the nymph's eyes.

sentences.t:
illa quidem tristis neque adhuc interrita vultu,
sed regina tamen, sed opaci maxima mundi,
sed tamen inferni pollens matrona tyranni.”
sentences.l:
she indeed sorrowful, and not yet unafraid in her face,
but a queen for all that, but the greatest of the shadowed world,
but for all that the powerful consort of the tyrant below.”
sentences.i: sorrowful, yes, and with the fear not yet gone out of her face — but a queen for all that, the greatest in that shadowed world, the powerful consort of the lord below.”
sentences.n: Three clauses with no verb in any of them, each opened by 'sed' — a rising repetition that lifts her line by line from a frightened girl to a ruling wife. 'interrita' is 'un-terrified', so 'neque adhuc interrita' is a double negative English usually turns round: 'still frightened'. 'vultu' is an ablative of respect, 'in respect of her face'. 'opaci maxima mundi' is a superlative with a partitive genitive, 'greatest of the dark world'. 'matrona' is the Roman word for a wife of standing, not a concubine, and 'tyrannus' in Latin verse is simply an absolute ruler, without the moral colour the English word carries. This is the one thing that can console a mother, and it is also the thing that makes the loss final.

sentences.t:
Mater ad auditas stupuit ceu saxea voces
attonitaeque diu similis fuit.
sentences.l:
The mother at the words heard was stunned as if made of stone,
and for a long time was like a woman thunderstruck.
sentences.i: At the words she heard, the mother stood stunned as though turned to stone, and for a long while was like a woman struck by lightning.
sentences.n: 'ad auditas voces' packs a clause into a participle: 'at the words [once they had been] heard'. Latin does this constantly and English almost always has to unpack it. 'ceu' is a poetic 'as if'. 'saxea' is made of rock — in a poem of transformations the comparison is nearly a threat. 'attonitus' is literally 'thundered at', and 'similis' takes a genitive or a dative of what a thing is like; 'attonitae' is feminine, 'like a woman thunderstruck'.

sentences.t:
Utque dolore
pulsa gravi gravis est amentia, curribus oras
exit in aetherias.
sentences.l:
And when by heavy grief
her heavy madness was driven out, with her chariot she goes out
into the airy regions.
sentences.i: And as soon as heavy grief had driven the heavy derangement out of her, she rode out in her chariot into the upper air.
sentences.n: 'gravi... gravis' — the same adjective given first to the grief and then to the madness, set side by side in the middle of the line so that the two weights touch. 'pulsa est' is perfect passive, 'was struck out, driven off'. 'amentia' is 'a-mentia', being out of one's mind. 'curribus' is a poetic plural for a single chariot, a habit of Latin verse with things made of parts. 'oras... aetherias', 'the shores of the upper air', is again split around the verb; 'ora' is a coast or margin, so the sky is a shore she puts out for.

sentences.t:
Ibi toto nubila vultu
ante Iovem passis stetit invidiosa capillis
sentences.l:
There, clouded over her whole face,
before Jupiter she stood, full of grievance, her hair let loose,
sentences.i: There she stood before Jupiter, her whole face clouded over, her hair hanging loose, the picture of a wrong done to her,
sentences.n: 'passis... capillis' is an ablative absolute — a phrase complete in itself, 'with her hair spread out' — where English wants a clause or a 'with' phrase; you will meet the construction on every page of Latin. 'passis' is from 'pando', to spread open, not from 'patior', to suffer: loosened hair is the standing sign of a woman in mourning or in supplication. 'nubila... vultu' is cloudy in respect of her face, the same ablative of respect as at 506. 'invidiosa' faces both ways in Latin — it can mean envied, and it can mean provoking ill-will — and here it is a woman who means her wrong to be seen.

sentences.t:
“pro” que “meo veni supplex tibi, Iuppiter” inquit,
“sanguine proque tuo.
sentences.l:
and “For my” — “I have come to you as a suppliant, Jupiter,” she says —
“blood, and for yours.
sentences.i: and said: “I come to you as a suppliant, Jupiter, for my own blood and for yours.
sentences.n: The printed page shows what Ovid is doing. Ceres' opening phrase is 'pro meo... sanguine proque tuo', 'for my blood and for yours', and it is torn in half by the narrator's 'inquit' ('she says') and by the rest of her own sentence, so that 'pro' and 'sanguine' end up in different lines. The '-que' printed outside the quotation marks after 'pro' is the narrator's connective, joining 'stetit' in the line before to 'inquit' here — an 'and' welded onto the first word of somebody else's speech. 'sanguis' is blood in the sense of offspring, one's own flesh: she speaks of the daughter without naming her. 'pro... supplex' repeats the construction Arethusa used at 493, where she said she was not pleading for a country of her own.

sentences.t:
Si nulla est gratia matris,
nata patrem moveat, neu sit tibi cura, precamur,
vilior illius, quod nostro est edita partu.
sentences.i: If a mother counts for nothing with you, let a daughter move her father; and I beg you, do not hold her the cheaper because it was I who bore her.
sentences.n: 'gratia matris' is an objective genitive — not the mother's favour but favour towards the mother, the credit a mother has with him. 'moveat' and 'sit' are jussive subjunctives, the mood Latin uses for 'let it...'. 'vilior' is a market word, 'of lower price', and it is held over the line-break from 'cura' so that the sentence lands on the reason: because she came out of my labour. 'precamur' is the plural for singular again, dropped in as a parenthesis. 'edita' is from 'edo', to put forth, the ordinary verb for bringing a child into the world.

sentences.t:
En quaesita diu tandem mihi nata reperta est,
si reperire vocas amittere certius, aut si
scire, ubi sit, reperire vocas.
sentences.l:
Look — the daughter long sought is at last found by me,
if you call losing her more surely 'finding', or if
you call knowing where she is 'finding'.
sentences.i: There: the daughter I hunted for so long has at last been found — if you call it finding to lose her more surely, or if you call it finding merely to know where she is.
sentences.n: 'En' is a pointing word, 'look', 'there you are'. The bitterness is worked with a single verb: 'reperta est... reperire... reperire', three times over and emptier each time. 'amittere certius' is 'to lose more certainly', with the comparative adverb — knowing where the girl is has made the loss definite rather than undone it. 'mihi' with the perfect passive 'reperta est' is the dative of agent, ordinary in verse: 'found by me'. 'ubi sit' is an indirect question with the subjunctive, as at 474.

sentences.t:
Quod rapta, feremus,
dummodo reddat eam: neque enim praedone marito
filia digna tua est, si iam mea filia non est.”
sentences.l:
That she was carried off, we shall bear,
provided he give her back: for your daughter is not worthy
of a bandit for a husband — if she is no longer my daughter.”
sentences.i: That she was carried off I will bear, so long as he gives her back. For your daughter does not deserve a bandit for a husband — if she is no longer mine.”
sentences.n: 'Quod rapta [est]' is a 'quod'-clause of fact standing as the object of 'feremus': 'the fact that she was seized'. 'dummodo' introduces a proviso and takes the subjunctive, 'provided only that he give her back'. 'praedone marito' is two ablative nouns side by side after 'digna' ('worthy of'), one in apposition to the other: a robber as a husband. 'praedo' is a plunderer, a brigand, a pirate — it is Ceres' name for the man who took her daughter, and it is set against 'gener', son-in-law, the word Jupiter answers with at 526. Her last clause is the sharpest: she will give up her own claim on the girl if that is what it takes to shame his.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter excepit: “Commune est pignus onusque
nata mihi tecum.
sentences.l:
Jupiter took her up: “Shared is the pledge and the burden,
the daughter, for me with you.
sentences.i: Jupiter answered: “The girl is a pledge we hold in common, and a charge we share.
sentences.n: 'excipio' is to catch something as it falls and so to take up what has just been said — the ordinary verb for answering in a dialogue. 'pignus' is a security, something handed over to guarantee a bond, and it is also the everyday Latin word for a child; 'onus' is a load, a charge. Putting the two together, his first move is to make the daughter a joint holding, and to concede in passing that she is trouble. 'commune... mihi tecum', 'shared, for me with you', is the arithmetic he wants: not her daughter, but theirs.

sentences.i: But if we are willing to give things their true names, what was done here is not an outrage; it is love;
sentences.n: 'nomina... vera', true names, is split around 'rebus addere', which is how a line of Latin verse is ordinarily built. 'placet' is impersonal, 'it is pleasing', with the infinitive as its subject. 'verum' at the head of the third line is the conjunction 'but', and it is the same stem as 'vera', 'true', two lines above — the word for truth doing two jobs while he renames what happened. 'iniuria' is taken here as a predicate noun, 'this deed is not an injury'; it can also be read as an ablative, 'this was not done wrongfully'. Either way the argument is one and the same, and it answers 'rapina' at 492 and 'praedo' at 521 by changing the vocabulary rather than the facts.

sentences.t:
neque erit nobis gener ille pudori,
tu modo, diva, velis.
sentences.l:
nor will that son-in-law be for a disgrace to us,
only let you be willing, goddess.
sentences.i: and that son-in-law will be no disgrace to us — only be willing, goddess.
sentences.n: 'nobis... pudori' is the double dative: one dative of the person concerned, 'to us', and one of the effect produced, 'for a disgrace' — a pairing Latin uses constantly with 'esse', which English renders with a plain 'be no disgrace to us'. 'gener' is son-in-law, and the whole argument is in that one noun: the word turns a seizure into a marriage. 'tu modo... velis' is a subjunctive tacked on as a condition, 'only let you be willing', so that the mother's consent is asked for after the fact.

sentences.t:
Ut desint cetera, quantum est
esse Iovis fratrem! —
sentences.l:
Granted that everything else be lacking — how much it is
to be Jupiter's brother! —
sentences.i: Even suppose all the rest were missing — what a thing it is to be the brother of Jupiter! —
sentences.n: 'ut' with the subjunctive is concessive here: 'granted that, suppose that'. 'quantum est' is an exclamation, 'how great a thing it is', and its subject is the infinitive phrase 'esse Iovis fratrem'; 'fratrem' is accusative because it is the predicate of the unexpressed accusative subject of 'esse'. Jupiter names himself in the third person and makes himself the measure of the match — and the dash this edition prints marks him pulling himself up short.

sentences.t:
Quid quod non cetera desunt
nec cedit nisi sorte mihi?
sentences.l:
What of the fact that the rest are not lacking,
and that he yields to me in nothing except the lot?
sentences.i: And what about the fact that nothing else is missing either, and that he is behind me only in the draw?
sentences.n: 'Quid quod...' is a debating move — 'what of the fact that...' — used to add a stronger point on top of a weaker one. 'cedo' takes a dative of the person given way to: 'cedit mihi', 'he is my inferior'. 'sorte' is an ablative of respect, 'in respect of the lot': the three brothers drew for the sky, the sea and the world below, and the whole of Jupiter's advantage over the man he is defending is that one draw.

sentences.t:
sed tanta cupido
si tibi discidii est, repetet Proserpina caelum,
sentences.l:
but if you have so great a longing
for the separation, Proserpina will make for the sky again,
sentences.i: but if you want the marriage broken as badly as that, Proserpina shall go back up to the sky —
sentences.n: 'tibi... est' is the dative of possession: Latin says 'there is to you a longing' where English says 'you have one'. 'cupido' and its genitive 'discidii' are split across the line-break. 'discidium' is a tearing apart, and it is the ordinary Roman word for a divorce — which tells you what Jupiter has already decided the arrangement is. 'repetet' is future, and 'caelum' the sky as the upper world in general.

sentences.t:
lege tamen certa, si nullos contigit illic
ore cibos; nam sic Parcarum foedere cautum est.”
sentences.l:
on a fixed term, however: if she has touched no food there
with her mouth; for so it has been provided by the compact of the Fates.”
sentences.i: on one fixed condition, though: that she has put no food there to her lips. That is the provision laid down in the Fates' compact.”
sentences.n: The vocabulary of the whole speech is contract law, and here it is unmixed: 'lex' is a term or clause of an agreement, 'foedus' a treaty, and 'cautum est' the technical verb for what a contract does when it stipulates or provides against something. 'lege... certa' is an ablative of the terms on which. 'si' here comes close to 'provided that'. 'contigit' is the perfect of 'contingo', to touch, and 'ore' an ablative of means. The Parcae are the Fates, and the point of naming them is that this is the one clause Jupiter cannot rewrite.

sentences.t: Dixerat. At Cereri certum est educere natam.
sentences.l: He had spoken. But for Ceres it is settled to lead her daughter out.
sentences.i: He had finished. But Ceres was set on bringing her daughter up out of there.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' standing alone is the regular Latin way of closing a speech — a pluperfect, 'he had done speaking'. 'certum est' with a dative and an infinitive means 'it is fixed for X to do Y', so 'Ceres is resolved to'. 'educere' is to lead out or up, the verb for fetching something from below. The tense slips from pluperfect into the present inside a single line, and the story is suddenly moving fast.

sentences.t:
Non ita fata sinunt, quoniam ieiunia virgo
solverat
sentences.l: Not so do the fates allow, since the girl had loosed her fastings
sentences.i: The Fates will not have it on those terms — the girl had already broken her fast
sentences.n: 'ita' means 'so, on those terms', and points back to the condition Jupiter has just laid down at 531–532. 'ieiunia solvere' is the standing idiom, 'to loosen the fast'; the plural 'ieiunia' is Latin's habit of putting an abstract in the plural without meaning more than one of them. 'virgo' is the unmarried girl. 'solverat' is pluperfect: the thing that decides the case was done long before the case was argued.

sentences.t:
et, cultis dum simplex errat in hortis,
Poeniceum curva decerpserat arbore pomum
sumptaque pallenti septem de cortice grana
presserat ore suo.
sentences.l:
and, while she wanders guileless in the tended gardens,
had plucked a Punic apple from a bent tree
and, seven grains taken from the pale rind,
had crushed them with her mouth.
sentences.i: and, while she was wandering, suspecting nothing, in the tended gardens, had picked a pomegranate from a bowed tree, taken seven seeds out of the pale rind, and crushed them in her mouth.
sentences.n: 'dum' keeps a present tense ('errat', she wanders) inside a sentence whose other verbs are pluperfect — a rule of the conjunction, not a shift of time, and English has to make it past. 'simplex' is 'once-folded', single, and so unsuspecting: the whole disaster sits in one adjective. 'Poeniceum... pomum' is the Punic apple, the Carthaginian apple — the pomegranate. 'curva... arbore' is an ablative of separation with 'decerpserat', the tree bent under the weight of its fruit. 'sumpta... grana' is a participle where English wants a second verb, 'and she took'. Three pluperfects — 'solverat', 'decerpserat', 'presserat' — put the act beyond recall before anyone begins to argue about it.

sentences.t:
Solusque ex omnibus illud
Ascalaphus vidit, quem quondam dicitur Orphne,
inter Avernales haud ignotissima nymphas,
ex Acheronte suo silvis peperisse sub atris:
sentences.l:
And alone out of them all Ascalaphus
saw it — he whom once Orphne,
not the least known among the nymphs of Avernus,
is said to have borne to her own Acheron beneath black woods:
sentences.i: And of them all only Ascalaphus saw it — Ascalaphus, whom Orphne, no obscure nymph among those of Avernus, is said once to have borne to her own Acheron under the black woods.
sentences.n: 'dicitur... peperisse' is the personal passive: Latin says 'she is said to have borne' where English may also say 'they say that she bore'. 'haud ignotissima' is litotes, a negated superlative meaning the opposite of what it says — 'not at all the least known', so quite well known indeed. Avernus is the lake counted as an entrance to the world below and Acheron one of its rivers, here treated as her mate: 'suo', her own. 'silvis sub atris' has the preposition inside its phrase, as Latin verse allows. 'solus ex omnibus' is what the rest of the story hangs on: one witness.

sentences.t: vidit et indicio reditum crudelis ademit.
sentences.l: he saw, and, cruel, by his informing took her return away.
sentences.i: he saw — and cruelly, by laying information, took her way back from her.
sentences.n: 'vidit' is picked up again from 539 after the long parenthesis about his parents: the sentence restarts where it broke off, and the repetition is the point — seeing was all he did, and then he spoke. 'indicium' is the technical word for information laid against someone, the informer's act, and 'indicio' is an ablative of means. 'adimo' takes an accusative of the thing removed and a dative of the person it is taken from, which is left here to be understood. 'crudelis' is a nominative adjective where English wants an adverb, 'cruelly'.

sentences.t:
Ingemuit regina Erebi testemque profanam
fecit avem, sparsumque caput Phlegethontide lympha
in rostrum et plumas et grandia lumina vertit.
sentences.l:
The queen of Erebus groaned, and the witness she made an unhallowed
bird, and his head, sprinkled with Phlegethon's water,
she turned into a beak and feathers and great eyes.
sentences.i: The queen of Erebus groaned and turned the witness into an unhallowed bird: she sprinkled his head with water of the Phlegethon and changed it into a beak, feathers, and huge eyes.
sentences.n: 'facio' with two accusatives — 'testem... fecit avem', made the witness a bird. 'profanam' is feminine and so agrees with 'avem' — 'avis' is feminine whatever the bird — rather than with 'testem', which would be masculine of the male Ascalaphus: what she makes him is an unhallowed bird. The word is 'pro-fanum', outside the shrine, and it is her judgement on what he did. Erebus is the darkness below and Phlegethon its river of fire. 'sparsum caput... lympha' is a participle plus an ablative of means doing the work of a whole English clause. The change is worked on the single noun 'caput', head, which becomes three things at once, so that the whole transformation happens inside one word.

sentences.t:
Ille sibi ablatus fulvis amicitur in alis,
inque caput crescit, longosque reflectitur ungues
vixque movet natas per inertia bracchia pennas:
sentences.l:
He, carried off from himself, is wrapped about in tawny wings,
and grows into head, and is curved back as to his long claws,
and scarcely moves the feathers born along his sluggish arms:
sentences.i: Taken away from himself, he is clothed in tawny wings; he grows all head; his nails curve back into long talons; and he can barely move the feathers that have sprouted along his listless arms:
sentences.n: 'sibi ablatus' is 'carried off from himself', a dative of separation: the man is taken away from the man. 'amicitur' is the passive of 'amicio', to throw a cloak round someone, so the wings are put on him like a garment. 'longos... ungues' after the passive 'reflectitur' is the Greek accusative of respect: the verb says what is done, the accusative says in what part — 'he is bent back as to his long claws'. Latin verse borrows the construction from Greek and you will meet it often; English has to say 'in respect of' or recast the sentence. 'in caput crescit' is 'grows into head' — he becomes all head. 'natas... pennas' are feathers just born.

sentences.t:
foedaque fit volucris, venturi nuntia luctus,
ignavus bubo, dirum mortalibus omen.
sentences.l:
and he becomes a foul bird, the herald of grief to come,
the sluggish screech-owl, a dread omen for mortals.
sentences.i: and he becomes a loathsome bird, the announcer of grief to come — the sluggish owl, a fearful omen to mortals.
sentences.n: 'venturi... luctus' is a future participle used as an adjective, grief 'that is going to come'. 'nuntia' is feminine because 'volucris', bird, is feminine in Latin whatever the bird's sex, and the noun means a messenger or an announcement: his punishment is to be, permanently, the thing he did once. 'bubo' is the eagle-owl or screech-owl, in Roman belief a bird whose cry announced a death. 'dirum... omen' stands in apposition, with 'mortalibus' in the dative. The line is unusually heavy — spondees almost the whole way, only the fifth foot running quick — and it drags like the creature it names.

sentences.t:
Hic tamen indicio poenam linguaque videri
commeruisse potest:
sentences.l:
He, at least, can seem to have fully earned his punishment
by informing and by his tongue:
sentences.i: He, at least, can be seen to have earned his punishment in full — he informed; he used his tongue.
sentences.n: Three verbs stacked together: 'potest videri commeruisse', 'he can seem to have deserved'. The 'com-' of 'commereo' is intensive, to earn thoroughly. 'indicio linguaque' is hendiadys — two nouns joined by 'and' where the sense is one thing, 'by the information his tongue laid'. 'Hic tamen' plants a contrast which the next sentence collects: he had it coming; the ones about to be addressed did not.

sentences.t:
vobis, Acheloides, unde
pluma pedesque avium, cum virginis ora geratis?
sentences.l:
for you, daughters of Achelous, from where
the feathers and the feet of birds, when you wear the face of a maiden?
sentences.i: But you, daughters of Achelous — where did your plumage and your birds' feet come from, when the face you wear is a girl's?
sentences.n: The poem turns from the story and speaks straight to the Sirens. This is apostrophe — the telling turning aside to address its own characters directly — and it runs unbroken from here to 563. 'Acheloides' is a Greek patronymic, 'the daughters of Achelous', a river-god. There is no verb in 'unde pluma pedesque avium': Latin leaves 'est' and 'sunt' out freely, and the bare question is the sharper for it. 'vobis' is a dative of possession, 'whence are the feathers to you'. 'cum... geratis' is concessive, 'although you wear', and 'ora' is plural because there is one face each.

sentences.t:
an quia, cum legeret vernos Proserpina flores,
in comitum numero, doctae Sirenes, eratis?
sentences.l:
or because, when Proserpina was gathering the flowers of spring,
you were in the number of her companions, learned Sirens?
sentences.i: Or is it because, when Proserpina was picking the flowers of spring, you were among her companions, you skilled Sirens?
sentences.n: 'an' introduces the second limb of a question — 'or is it because...?' — and here the question supplies its own answer. 'cum legeret' is circumstantial 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive, 'at the time when she was gathering'. 'lego' is to pick up or gather, the same verb used of the greedy birds gathering seed at 485. 'in comitum numero', 'in the number of her companions', is Latin's ordinary way of saying 'among'. 'doctae' means trained, skilled — the epithet given them just before the poem explains that the voice is the one thing they kept.

sentences.t:
Quam postquam toto frustra quaesistis in orbe,
protinus, ut vestram sentirent aequora curam,
posse super fluctus alarum insistere remis
optastis,
sentences.l:
And after you had sought her in vain over the whole world,
at once, so that the seas might feel your care,
you wished to be able to stand on the oars of wings above the waves,
sentences.i: And when you had searched the whole world for her in vain, at once — so that the seas too might feel your care — you wished you could stand above the waves on the oars of your wings,
sentences.n: 'Quam' opens the sentence as a connecting relative: 'and her', meaning Proserpina. 'quaesistis' and 'optastis' are the shortened perfects for 'quaesivistis' and 'optavistis', normal in verse and worth recognising on sight. 'alarum remis', 'with the oars of wings', is a metaphor Latin builds out of a bare genitive where English needs 'like oars'. 'insistere' is to plant oneself on something. Magnus prints 'ut... sentirent', a purpose clause — 'so that the seas might feel your care'; a second witness prints 'et' in its place, which leaves the subjunctive 'sentirent' with no conjunction to govern it.

sentences.t:
facilesque deos habuistis et artus
vidistis vestros subitis flavescere pennis.
sentences.l:
and you had the gods obliging, and you saw
your own limbs turn yellow with sudden feathers.
sentences.i: and you found the gods obliging, and watched your own limbs turn golden with feathers that came all at once.
sentences.n: 'facilesque deos habuistis', 'you had the gods easy', is an object plus a predicate adjective — Latin's compact way of saying that a prayer was granted. 'vidistis... artus... flavescere' is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving: you saw your limbs grow yellow. 'flavesco' carries the inceptive '-sc-' ending, which marks a process beginning: not 'be yellow' but 'turn yellow'. The second person runs on — the change is being narrated to the ones it happened to.

sentences.t:
Ne tamen ille canor mulcendas natus ad aures
tantaque dos oris linguae deperderet usum,
virginei vultus et vox humana remansit.
sentences.l:
Yet, lest that singing, born for ears to be soothed,
and so great a dowry of the mouth, should lose the use of the tongue,
maidenly faces and a human voice remained.
sentences.i: Yet so that that singing of theirs, born to charm the ear, and so rich a gift of mouth, should not lose the use of a tongue, the girls' faces and the human voice stayed.
sentences.n: 'Ne... deperderet' is a negative purpose clause, 'so that it should not lose'. 'mulcendas... ad aures' is a gerundive of purpose after 'ad', 'towards ears to be soothed', which English says as 'to charm the ear'. 'dos' is the dowry a bride brings, used here of a natural endowment: what these women bring with them is a voice. 'deperderet' is singular although it has two subjects, 'canor' and 'dos', agreeing with the nearer one, and 'remansit' does the same at the end. 'virginei vultus' is nominative plural — a face each, as at 553 — beside the singular 'vox humana'. This is where the whole address lands — the bird took everything except the voice.

sentences.t:
At medius fratrisque sui maestaeque sororis
Iuppiter ex aequo volventem dividit annum.
sentences.l:
But Jupiter, midway of his own brother and his grieving sister,
divides the rolling year on equal terms.
sentences.i: But Jupiter, standing midway between his brother and his grieving sister, divides the turning year evenly between them.
sentences.n: 'medius' takes two genitives where English needs 'between': 'in the middle of his brother and his sister'. Ceres is Jupiter's sister as well as the mother of his daughter, and the line puts the whole quarrel back inside one family. 'ex aequo' is a fixed phrase, 'on equal terms'. 'volventem... annum' is the year rolling round of itself — an active form with a middle sense, turning itself. The verdict takes one line, and nobody is consulted.

sentences.t:
Nunc dea, regnorum numen commune duorum,
cum matre est totidem, totidem cum coniuge menses.
sentences.l:
Now the goddess, a shared divinity of two kingdoms,
is with her mother so many months, so many with her husband.
sentences.i: Now the goddess, a power held in common by two kingdoms, spends as many months with her mother as she does with her husband.
sentences.n: 'numen commune... duorum regnorum' stands in apposition to 'dea': she is no longer a girl who was taken but an institution two realms share. 'totidem... totidem' is 'just so many... just as many' — the balance is stated by repeating the word, and no number is ever given. 'menses' is an accusative of duration of time. 'nunc' and the present tense leave the arrangement standing to this day. And the word for the man is now 'coniux', husband: set that beside 'praedo', bandit, at 521, and the distance the argument has travelled is one noun.

sentences.t: Vertitur extemplo facies et mentis et oris:
sentences.l: At once the face both of her mind and of her countenance is turned:
sentences.i: At once her whole aspect changes — of mind as much as of face:
sentences.n: 'facies' covers both the look of a face and the cast of a mind, and 'et... et' ('both... and') yokes the two genitives to it. 'vertitur' is the same verb used at 545 of turning Ascalaphus's head into a beak and feathers: the word for a body remade is used here of nothing more than a change of mood. 'extemplo' is on the spot, immediately.

sentences.t:
nam modo quae poterat Diti quoque maesta videri,
laeta deae frons est, ut sol, qui tectus aquosis
nubibus ante fuit, victis e nubibus exit.
sentences.l:
for the brow of the goddess, which a moment ago could seem
sorrowful even to Dis, is glad — as the sun, which was covered before
by watery clouds, comes out from the clouds it has beaten.
sentences.i: for the goddess's face, which only a moment before could look sorrowful even to Dis, is bright now — like the sun, hidden till then behind rain-clouds, breaking out of the clouds it has beaten.
sentences.n: 'quae' is feminine and looks forward to a noun that has not arrived yet: 'frons', the brow, which turns up only in the next line. Latin can put the relative clause first and let its antecedent follow; English has to name the thing before it can describe it. 'Diti quoque' is 'even to Dis' — the adverb 'quoque', 'also, even', with the dative that 'videri', 'to seem to someone', requires; watch that word, because the same letters can also be 'quo-que', 'and with which'. 'poterat... videri' is imperfect, 'could seem'. 'victis e nubibus' packs a battle into one participle: the clouds are beaten. The story of a goddess who took the harvest away from the world ends on the weather clearing.

questions: House-rendering candidate, 463: 'quaerenti defuit orbis' is a quotable tag and I shipped literal 'to her, seeking, the world ran short' / idiomatic 'she ran out of world to search in'. Built from the grammar (desum + dative); please ratify or replace before it spreads.
House-rendering candidate, 527-528: 'quantum est / esse Iovis fratrem!' shipped as 'what a thing it is to be the brother of Jupiter!'. Much-quoted line; ratify.

House-rendering candidate, 566-567: 'cum matre est totidem, totidem cum coniuge menses' shipped as 'spends as many months with her mother as she does with her husband'. This is the aetiology line everyone quotes; ratify.

Interpretive call, 514: Magnus prints the enclitic '-que' outside the quotation marks ('pro' que 'meo veni...'). I construed it as the narrator's connective joining 'stetit' (513) to 'inquit' (514), welded orthographically onto the first word of Ceres' speech, and the note says so. The alternative — reading 'proque' as part of the speech — leaves the '-que' coordinating nothing. Worth a second eye.

Interpretive call, 525: 'non hoc iniuria factum' — I took 'iniuria' as a predicate nominative ('this deed is not an injury'), parallel to 'verum amor est', and flagged the ablative reading ('this was not done wrongfully') in the note. Confirm which we want standing.

Advisory call: I fired the sexual-violence trigger in object form even though the seizure is narrated in the preceding part (V.385-461) rather than here. This part argues about it, renames it, and settles it, and a reader opening the poem at 462 meets a girl made a wife without being asked. If the batch rule is that the advisory belongs only to the part that narrates the act, strike it.

Variant, 557: Magnus prints 'ut vestram sentirent aequora curam' (purpose clause); the second witness reads 'et', which turns it into a statement. Flagged in the note — the only one of the four flagged variants in this part that changes the sense (471 tunc/tum, 528 non/nec and 536 Poeniceum/puniceum do not, and carry no note).

Metrical claim, 550: the note calls 'ignavus bubo, dirum mortalibus omen' spondaic almost throughout with only the fifth foot quick. I scanned it as four spondees, dactyl, spondee. Review re-scanned it independently and got the same — ig-na | vus bu | bo di | rum mor | ta-li-bus | o-men — so the note stands; no further check needed.

House-rendering candidate, 525-526 (added at review): 'non hoc iniuria factum, verum amor est' is the hinge of the part and a much-quoted sententia. Shipped as literal 'this deed is not an injury but love' / idiomatic 'what was done here is not an outrage; it is love'. Ratify with the other three.

Review call, 543-544: 'testemque profanam ... fecit avem'. Review moved 'profanam' off the witness and onto 'avem', on the gender — 'testis' is common gender and would be masculine of the male Ascalaphus, while 'profanam' is feminine and 'avis' is feminine. The proleptic reading ('made the profane witness a bird') is defensible and was what the drafter shipped; confirm which we want standing.

Review verdict on the advisory: kept, unchanged. The seizure is narrated in V.385-461, but these lines name it three times ('raptam' 471, 'rapinae' 492, 'rapta' 520), argue it ('praedone marito' 521 against 'gener' 526), rename it ('non hoc iniuria factum, verum amor est' 525-526) and dispose of the girl's year without her (564-567).
